subject: Careers
scope: Autumn 1 · Weeks 1–7 · Identity & Belonging — Knowing myself
intro: Seven original 40-minute lessons adapted from the supplied Careers slides, pathway pupil resources, teacher resources and Build_Grow_Careers_SoW_2026-27.xlsx. Each pathway follows its own weekly outcomes. Profiles are provisional and reviewed as experience grows. Pupils may use the named fictional cases throughout; label these as case analysis rather than personal employment evidence. These classroom materials do not award a qualification or establish whole-school careers-guidance compliance.

sources.title: Uploaded Careers scheme and lesson resources
sources.note: Build_Grow_Careers_SoW_2026-27.xlsx, GROW Careers sheet, Autumn 1 rows; Careers_Lesson_1–7_Build_Grow.pptx and matching pupil/teacher DOCX. The supplied Compliance Map is contextual planning, not verified evidence that a benchmark or statutory duty is met.

sources.title: National Careers Service — Explore careers

sources.title: National Careers Service — Discover your skills and careers
sources.note: Checked 7 September 2026. Career suggestions are starting points to compare, not a prediction or instruction. No pupil account, questionnaire or personal disclosure is required in this pack.

sources.title: National Careers Service — Understand and develop your skills

lessons.title: Career development: where am I now?
lessons.big_question: How do evidence, choices and circumstances shape a career journey?
lessons.objective: I can explain how careers develop over time and record my current aspirations and uncertainties.
success: I can compare two changing career journeys.
I can separate stated evidence from an assumption.
I can record an aspiration or uncertainty and a useful enquiry question.

vocabulary.meaning: How learning, work and decisions change through life.
Something a person may want to achieve or explore.
Something not yet known or decided.
A purposeful investigation that can inform a decision.

slides.title: Career development: where am I now?
body: How do evidence, choices and circumstances shape a career journey?
I can explain how careers develop over time and record my current aspirations and uncertainties.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct GROW Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: “Your first job decides your whole career.” Agree or disagree?
What information might change a career plan?
slides.prompt: Give a reason; do not share personal history unless you choose.
slides.answer: Disagree. Learning, opportunities, interests and circumstances can change a route.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: A route can develop
body: A career is broader than one job or qualification.
A change of direction is not automatically failure.
A good enquiry asks what evidence is missing.
slides.prompt: Does a case study prove that a route is available to everyone?
slides.answer: No. It illustrates a possibility; actual entry routes and circumstances need checking.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 7 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Compare Jamie and Morgan
body: Jamie: practical learning → apprenticeship → trade work → supervision and further learning.
Morgan: art and college → retail work while learning design tools → junior design work.
Both are fictional illustrations, not recommended or guaranteed routes.
slides.prompt: What changes, and what seems to continue?
slides.answer: Jamie’s responsibilities change while practical problem-solving remains relevant. Morgan changes work area while creative/digital interests continue. Neither sequence proves a universal route.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Trace evidence and unknowns
body: Jamie undertakes more training after starting work.
Morgan combines a job with learning another skill.
Neither card states pay, age, provider or guaranteed entry criteria.
slides.prompt: Write one supported comparison and one unknown.
slides.answer: Both continue learning; Morgan changes sector while Jamie moves into supervision. Exact qualifications and access to routes remain unknown.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: A useful enquiry question
body: A: “Will I definitely be successful?”
B: “What tasks and training does this role involve?”
slides.prompt: Which question can guide an investigation?
slides.answer: B can be checked against current role information and provider advice; A asks for an impossible guarantee.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Compare the two journeys: Use the full Jamie and Morgan cards.
2. Make a starting-point record: Choose personal reflection or analyse Morgan as a fictional case.
3. Set an enquiry question: Record an idea, an uncertainty and a question that could change your thinking.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 13 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can compare two changing career journeys.
I can separate stated evidence from an assumption.
I can record an aspiration or uncertainty and a useful enquiry question.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when the pupil explains change using both cases and records a baseline or clearly labelled case analysis plus a focused enquiry. Do not grade readiness confidence or certainty of ambition.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Career-readiness baseline, aspiration record and enquiry question.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Explain one reason careers can change and write one investigable question.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: Further learning may lead to different tasks or roles. “What tasks are common in two design roles?” can be investigated; a guaranteed outcome cannot.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: Career development: where am I now? — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Compare the two journeys
tasks.prompt: Use the full Jamie and Morgan cards.
items: Identify one change in each route.
Identify one interest or skill that stays relevant.
Give one similarity, one difference and one fact the cards do not supply.
tasks.answer: Jamie: trade work to supervision, continued practical skills. Morgan: retail to design, creative/digital interests. Both keep learning; the pattern of change differs. No pay or exact qualification details are given.

tasks.heading: 2. Make a starting-point record
tasks.prompt: Choose personal reflection or analyse Morgan as a fictional case.
items: Three stages: past learning / now / possible next direction.
Readiness: explain a career / identify an area / identify a skill / name an information source.
For each readiness item use not yet / developing / more confident, or stated / unknown for Morgan.
tasks.answer: For Morgan the card supports a broad career explanation, creative/digital interest and ongoing learning. A preferred information source is unknown. Personal ratings are a baseline, not a marked test.

tasks.heading: 3. Set an enquiry question
tasks.prompt: Record an idea, an uncertainty and a question that could change your thinking.
items: I or Morgan might explore…
I still need to know…
A useful question is…
tasks.answer: Morgan might explore different design tasks. Unknown: which tasks and conditions fit. Question: How do typical tasks differ between two design roles?

worksheet.exit_question: Explain one reason careers can change and write one investigable question.
worksheet.exit_answer: Further learning may lead to different tasks or roles. “What tasks are common in two design roles?” can be investigated; a guaranteed outcome cannot.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: Jamie’s responsibilities change while practical problem-solving remains relevant. Morgan changes work area while creative/digital interests continue. Neither sequence proves a universal route. Both continue learning; Morgan changes sector while Jamie moves into supervision. Exact qualifications and access to routes remain unknown.
misconceptions: A career must be a straight line → compare the two routes.
Changing direction means failure → the cards show learning and exploration.
One case proves a route for all → actual requirements and circumstances need checking.
teacher.support: Provide a two-column change/continuity grid; underline the action words. Use Morgan for the timeline if a personal account would be intrusive. Fade sentence stems after one example.
teacher.stretch: Explain two possible causes of career change while distinguishing evidence in the card from a reasonable but unconfirmed possibility.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when the pupil explains change using both cases and records a baseline or clearly labelled case analysis plus a focused enquiry. Do not grade readiness confidence or certainty of ambition.

resources.title: Jamie and Morgan — complete journeys
resources.instructions: Both people and journeys are fictional teaching examples. They are not route guarantees or live course information.
items: Jamie enjoyed practical problem-solving at school. Jamie later began an apprenticeship, worked in a trade, took on supervision and continued learning about safe work.
Morgan enjoyed art and computers. After college, Morgan worked in retail while practising design software, then moved into junior digital-design work and continued learning.
The cases omit exact dates, ages, providers, qualifications, pay and individual support arrangements.
A reader can compare the changes but must not invent the missing details.
answers: Jamie changes responsibility; Morgan changes work area.
Both continue learning.
Interests and skills inform exploration without fixing a person’s route.

resources.title: Baseline and question-builder cards
resources.instructions: Personal ratings may stay private. For a fictional case use stated / unknown instead of claiming personal confidence.
items: Can explain job and career.
Can name an area worth exploring.
Can name a skill with evidence.
Can identify a source or person to ask.
Question stem: What does the role involve?
Question stem: What learning routes or support should I investigate?
Question stem: What new information might change this shortlist?
answers: A baseline identifies a next learning need; it does not rank pupils.
A useful question is specific enough to investigate and leaves room for a changed view.

lessons.title: Strengths with evidence
lessons.big_question: What makes a strength claim credible?
lessons.objective: I can identify at least four strengths and give credible evidence for two.
success: I can identify four strengths.
I can support two with a context and specific action.
I can distinguish an evidenced claim from an exaggeration or qualification.

vocabulary.meaning: A statement that needs supporting information.
Specific and believable without exaggeration.
The situation in which an action happened.
A formal award or certificate; it is not the same as a strength.

slides.title: Strengths with evidence
body: What makes a strength claim credible?
I can identify at least four strengths and give credible evidence for two.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct GROW Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: A: “I am excellent at everything.”
B: “I checked each label against the list and corrected two errors.”
slides.prompt: Which gives more useful evidence?
slides.answer: B names a specific action and result. It can support carefulness without proving every skill.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Build a credible statement
body: Name a strength, a context and what the person actually did.
Add a result only when it is known.
One example supports a claim; it does not prove “always” or “perfect”.
slides.prompt: Can a strong statement include support?
slides.answer: Yes. “Using a checklist, I…” can accurately describe a skill and its conditions.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 7 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Rowan’s project audit
body: Rowan sorted cards, checked labels and corrected two errors.
When the layout failed, Rowan used a grid and revised it.
Rowan explained the revised layout to a partner.
slides.prompt: Which four strengths are supported?
slides.answer: Organisation, carefulness, persistence/problem-solving and communication. The actions support each; no formal qualification is described.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Upgrade the claim
body: Weak: “Rowan is organised.”
Stronger: “During the display task Rowan grouped the cards before planning the layout.”
Known result: the revised layout fitted the board.
slides.prompt: Write a second statement using different evidence.
slides.answer: Rowan showed carefulness by checking every label and correcting two errors. Keep the claim proportionate.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: Keep it accurate
body: A: “This proves Rowan will always meet every deadline.”
B: “This task gives evidence of planning and checking.”
slides.prompt: Which avoids exaggeration?
slides.answer: B. No deadline record or long-term pattern is supplied.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Audit four strengths: Choose yourself or Rowan; identify an evidence context for each.
2. Write two credible statements: Include strength + context + action; add a known result where helpful.
3. Check the limits and next step: Identify a vague or exaggerated claim, then set one development action.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 13 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can identify four strengths.
I can support two with a context and specific action.
I can distinguish an evidenced claim from an exaggeration or qualification.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when four strengths are identified and two supported by specific credible evidence. Check proportionate language, honest use of support and separate labelling of fictional analysis.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Skills audit with evidence examples.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Write one evidence statement and explain why it is credible.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: “During the display task Rowan checked labels and corrected two mismatches” names a context, action and known result. It does not claim perfection.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: Strengths with evidence — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Audit four strengths
tasks.prompt: Choose yourself or Rowan; identify an evidence context for each.
items: Bank: organised, careful, creative, practical, patient, persistent, adaptable, reliable, communicative, helpful.
Four rows: strength / context or evidence still needed.
tasks.answer: Rowan: organised—sorted cards; careful—checked labels; persistent—revised layout; communication—explained it. Accept other supported labels.

tasks.heading: 2. Write two credible statements
tasks.prompt: Include strength + context + action; add a known result where helpful.
items: Statement 1…
Statement 2…
Mark personal example or fictional case analysis.
tasks.answer: Rowan was careful in the display project: checked labels and corrected two errors. Rowan showed persistence by using a grid and revising a layout that did not fit.

tasks.heading: 3. Check the limits and next step
tasks.prompt: Identify a vague or exaggerated claim, then set one development action.
items: What does your evidence support?
What does it not prove?
What small practice would help strengthen one area?
tasks.answer: Rowan’s evidence supports this project’s actions, not perfect reliability across all tasks or a qualification. Next: use and review a checklist in another task to gather further evidence.

worksheet.exit_question: Write one evidence statement and explain why it is credible.
worksheet.exit_answer: “During the display task Rowan checked labels and corrected two mismatches” names a context, action and known result. It does not claim perfection.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check

teacher.modelling: Organisation, carefulness, persistence/problem-solving and communication. The actions support each; no formal qualification is described. Rowan showed carefulness by checking every label and correcting two errors. Keep the claim proportionate.
misconceptions: A qualification and a strength are the same → one is an award, the other a capability or quality.
A good result must be invented → include only what is known.
Using support invalidates evidence → record support honestly alongside the person’s action.
teacher.support: Provide context/action/result boxes. Establish four labels together, then ask the learner to choose the evidence for two. Allow spoken rehearsal before writing.
teacher.stretch: Compare two plausible strengths for the same action and judge which is better supported; identify what extra observation would strengthen the other claim.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.

Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when four strengths are identified and two supported by specific credible evidence. Check proportionate language, honest use of support and separate labelling of fictional analysis.

resources.title: Rowan’s evidence record
resources.instructions: Complete fictional case. Use only stated facts when writing evidence.
items: In a classroom display project, Rowan sorted six cards into groups.
Rowan checked every label and corrected two mismatches.
The first layout did not fit. Rowan used a teacher-provided grid and revised it.
The revised arrangement fitted the board.
Rowan explained the changes to a partner.
There is no information about qualifications, attendance, employment or performance in other tasks.
answers: Four possible strengths: organisation, carefulness, persistence/problem-solving, communication.
Use of a grid is relevant support, not a reason to discount the action.
Do not infer formal qualifications or a universal personality trait.

resources.title: Evidence-quality comparison cards
resources.instructions: Rank by specificity, then state each claim’s limits.
items: A: “I am organised.”
B: “During the project I sorted the materials before starting.”
C: “I have a certificate.”
D: “I always solve every problem perfectly.”
E: “When the layout failed, I used the grid and revised it so the cards fitted.”
answers: B and E give specific actions; E includes a result.
A may be true but needs an example.
C refers to an unspecified award; it does not itself identify the demonstrated strength.
D is an unsupported absolute claim.

lessons.title: Interests, values and working preferences
lessons.big_question: How can priorities guide exploration without deciding everything?
lessons.objective: I can prioritise what matters to me in work and explain how this may affect the careers I explore.
success: I can rank five current priorities and explain two.
I can compare two fictional options using evidence.
I can identify a trade-off and an unknown without giving up fair treatment or safety.

vocabulary.meaning: An activity or topic that holds attention or curiosity.
Something that matters when considering work.
Something given more weight in a current decision.
A compromise between preferences; not surrendering dignity, safety or fair treatment.

slides.title: Interests, values and working preferences
body: How can priorities guide exploration without deciding everything?
I can prioritise what matters to me in work and explain how this may affect the careers I explore.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct GROW Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: Interest: enjoys creating posters. Preference: likes a calmer setting.
Can a person value both variety and predictable hours?
slides.prompt: Give a reason.
slides.answer: Yes. Different priorities can coexist; the person may need to compare how each option meets them.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Rank, explain, revisit
body: Interests suggest tasks to explore; values help judge what matters.
Preferences can change with experience or circumstances.
Safety, dignity and fair treatment are not optional bargaining items.
slides.prompt: What is the difference between a priority and a job requirement?
slides.answer: A priority matters to the person; a requirement is needed for a particular role. Both need checking, but they are not the same.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 7 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Maya’s two fictional placements
body: Maya values creativity, clear plans and quieter work.
A: create display layouts; steady timetable; repeated design tasks.
B: plan events; more variety and people contact; schedule changes.
slides.prompt: Which fits Maya’s stated priorities better?
slides.answer: A currently fits creativity, predictability and quieter work. It offers less task variety. These are fictional placements, not claims about whole sectors.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Compare the evidence
body: Maya also likes helping people, but it is not the top priority today.
B offers more direct group contact.
Neither card states pay, travel time or available adjustments.
slides.prompt: What changes if variety becomes Maya’s top priority?
slides.answer: B may deserve closer investigation. Maya would still need to check schedule changes and actual conditions; missing facts cannot be treated as poor fit.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: A fair trade-off?
body: A: less variety in exchange for a predictable pattern.
B: accepting humiliation to get a creative task.
slides.prompt: Which is a preference trade-off?
slides.answer: A. B is harmful treatment to challenge, not a normal career compromise.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Build a priorities profile: Use your own priorities or Maya’s card. Rank five and explain the top two.
2. Compare options A and B: Use two criteria and identify one unknown.
3. Test a change of priority: Explain a possible preference trade-off and how new evidence could change the choice.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 13 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can rank five current priorities and explain two.
I can compare two fictional options using evidence.
I can identify a trade-off and an unknown without giving up fair treatment or safety.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when five priorities are ordered, two explained, and a comparison includes evidence, a genuine preference trade-off and an unknown. There is no preferred personal ranking.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Prioritised career-values profile.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Explain one priority, one possible trade-off and one fact to check.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: Maya prioritises predictability and may accept less variety. Maya should check how schedule changes are communicated before deciding.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: Interests, values and working preferences — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Build a priorities profile
tasks.prompt: Use your own priorities or Maya’s card. Rank five and explain the top two.
items: Possible values: creativity, purpose, income, learning, stability, independence, teamwork, variety, predictable plans, location.
Record three working preferences: people/independent; steady/changing tasks; calmer/busier.
Both or unsure is allowed; identify what experience would help.
tasks.answer: Maya’s stated top priorities are creativity, predictable plans and quieter work; learning and helping are also present. Personal rankings have no single correct order. Safety and fair treatment are not ranked away.

tasks.heading: 2. Compare options A and B
tasks.prompt: Use two criteria and identify one unknown.
items: Which option currently fits the chosen profile better?
Which two details support that view?
What important information is absent?
tasks.answer: A fits Maya’s stated priorities through creative tasks and a steady calmer setting. Unknowns include travel, actual support and pay; cards are hypothetical and give no current wage information.

tasks.heading: 3. Test a change of priority
tasks.prompt: Explain a possible preference trade-off and how new evidence could change the choice.
items: A trade-off could be…
If the priority changed to… then…
Before choosing, ask…
tasks.answer: Maya may accept less variety for predictability. If variety becomes most important, B may merit investigation. Ask how often plans change and how changes are communicated.

worksheet.exit_question: Explain one priority, one possible trade-off and one fact to check.
worksheet.exit_answer: Maya prioritises predictability and may accept less variety. Maya should check how schedule changes are communicated before deciding.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: A currently fits creativity, predictability and quieter work. It offers less task variety. These are fictional placements, not claims about whole sectors. B may deserve closer investigation. Maya would still need to check schedule changes and actual conditions; missing facts cannot be treated as poor fit.
misconceptions: The highest income must be everyone’s top value → priorities and circumstances differ; do not require financial disclosure.
A trade-off includes accepting disrespect → separate preferences from fair treatment and safety.
Fictional conditions describe an entire sector → real roles vary.
teacher.support: Supply Maya’s profile and five priority cards. First compare two criteria, then add an unknown. Explain reasons orally before completing the grid.
teacher.stretch: Re-rank the options under two different priorities and explain why the evidence permits more than one reasonable judgement.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when five priorities are ordered, two explained, and a comparison includes evidence, a genuine preference trade-off and an unknown. There is no preferred personal ranking.

resources.title: Maya and the two fictional placements
resources.instructions: These are invented comparison options, not real vacancies, typical-sector claims or promises of a placement.
items: Maya enjoys creative tasks and making clear plans. Quieter conditions help concentration. Maya also likes learning and helping people.
Option A: create classroom display layouts in a calmer studio; a steady timetable; repeated design tasks; occasional group planning.
Option B: help plan community events; different tasks and frequent group contact; some noisy activity; changes in the schedule.
Both options are described as supervised, respectful learning settings. Actual access arrangements would need checking.
No pay, travel, age criteria or qualification requirements are supplied.
answers: A best matches Maya’s currently stated top priorities, with less variety as a possible trade-off.
B could become worth investigating if variety/group contact receives more weight.
Do not infer that design is always quiet or events always involve unpredictable hours.

resources.title: Priority and uncertainty cards
resources.instructions: Use to compare preferences without a job-predictor score.
items: Interest: what tasks attract your attention?
Value: what matters to you, such as purpose, learning or income?
Preference: what working pattern helps?
Evidence: what does the option actually say?
Unknown: what needs checking?
Boundary: dignity, safety and fair treatment remain expectations.
answers: A ranked list can change after experience.
An unknown is a research question, not a zero score or proof of poor fit.
Do not promise that every preferred condition will be available.

lessons.title: Identity, stereotypes and opportunity
lessons.big_question: How can we challenge assumptions and investigate real barriers?
lessons.objective: I can identify stereotypical thinking and explain why career choices should be based on evidence, interests and capability.
success: I can identify the group assumption in a stereotype.
I can distinguish a stereotype, a requirement and an access barrier.
I can suggest an evidence-based response without promising a solution.

vocabulary.meaning: A fixed assumption about a group of people.
An obstacle that makes access or participation harder.
Something genuinely needed for a particular role or task.
Being able to reach, enter or participate in an opportunity.

slides.title: Identity, stereotypes and opportunity
body: How can we challenge assumptions and investigate real barriers?
I can identify stereotypical thinking and explain why career choices should be based on evidence, interests and capability.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct GROW Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: A learner has no suitable bus route to a course.
Someone says the course is “not for people like you”.
slides.prompt: What is different about these statements?
slides.answer: The first describes a practical access barrier. The second is a group assumption that can itself create discouragement or exclusion.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Separate the issue, choose a response
body: Stereotype: replace group assumptions with individual evidence.
Requirement: check the actual role or provider information.
Barrier: investigate support or alternatives; do not assume a solution exists.
slides.prompt: Can a stereotype also create a barrier?
slides.answer: Yes. Categories can overlap: an assumption may lead to exclusion. Naming a practical barrier does not make discrimination harmless.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 7 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Kai’s vehicle-maintenance enquiry
body: Kai enjoys fault-finding and follows a checking sequence in practical tasks.
The provider is difficult to reach by public transport.
A comment says: “That course is not for people from your background.”
slides.prompt: Name the assumption, the barrier and the relevant evidence.
slides.answer: Background comment: stereotype. Transport: access barrier. Fault-finding and checking: relevant evidence. Actual training criteria still need checking.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Plan without guessing
body: Ask the provider about times, route options and any available travel support.
Ask a careers adviser about comparable providers or routes.
Keep the answer unknown until someone confirms the details.
slides.prompt: Which response makes an unsupported promise?
slides.answer: “The provider will definitely pay for taxis” is unsupported. Asking what help exists is appropriate.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: A requirement is not a stereotype
body: A: this named course lists a qualification not yet achieved.
B: people of one gender cannot learn these skills.
slides.prompt: How would your response differ?
slides.answer: A: check the current requirement and any alternative route with the provider. B: challenge the gender assumption and use individual evidence.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Classify and justify: Use stereotype / requirement / barrier; overlap is allowed if explained.
2. Rewrite an assumption: Choose one supplied example and replace the assumption with fair evidence-based reasoning.
3. Make a barrier enquiry plan: Use Kai’s full card. State obstacle, possible questions and who could confirm an answer.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 13 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can identify the group assumption in a stereotype.
I can distinguish a stereotype, a requirement and an access barrier.
I can suggest an evidence-based response without promising a solution.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when the pupil challenges an assumption with evidence, accurately identifies an obstacle or requirement, and proposes a specific enquiry with no unsupported guarantee.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Stereotype/barrier reflection and role-model note.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Give one stereotype, one real barrier and a sensible next question.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: A background-based judgement is a stereotype; transport is a barrier. Ask the provider which timetable or support options are actually available.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: Identity, stereotypes and opportunity — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Classify and justify
tasks.prompt: Use stereotype / requirement / barrier; overlap is allowed if explained.
items: No suitable transport route reaches the training centre.
An adult assumes a learner will be unreliable because of their background.
A fictional course lists a prerequisite not yet achieved.
A workplace entrance cannot be accessed by a visitor.
tasks.answer: Transport and inaccessible entrance: barriers. Background reliability assumption: stereotype, which may become a barrier. Prerequisite: stated course requirement and a current access hurdle; verify with the provider.

tasks.heading: 2. Rewrite an assumption
tasks.prompt: Choose one supplied example and replace the assumption with fair evidence-based reasoning.
items: Only one gender can do care or technical work.
A disability automatically rules out every demanding role.
A quiet person cannot contribute to a team.
tasks.answer: Suitability should be considered using individual interests, skills, actual tasks, training and access needs. Avoid the opposite overclaim that anyone can do every job regardless of requirements.

tasks.heading: 3. Make a barrier enquiry plan
tasks.prompt: Use Kai’s full card. State obstacle, possible questions and who could confirm an answer.
items: The real obstacle is…
Two questions to ask are…
A possible next contact/source is…
What remains unconfirmed?
tasks.answer: Transport is the obstacle. Ask provider about start times/travel support; ask school careers adviser about comparable routes. Availability, eligibility and suitability of any help remain unconfirmed.

worksheet.exit_question: Give one stereotype, one real barrier and a sensible next question.
worksheet.exit_answer: A background-based judgement is a stereotype; transport is a barrier. Ask the provider which timetable or support options are actually available.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: Background comment: stereotype. Transport: access barrier. Fault-finding and checking: relevant evidence. Actual training criteria still need checking. “The provider will definitely pay for taxis” is unsupported. Asking what help exists is appropriate.
misconceptions: Stereotypes and barriers never overlap → assumptions may create exclusion.
A barrier means a learner lacks ability → access and capability are different.
Support is guaranteed → investigate and confirm actual availability and suitability.
teacher.support: Colour-code assumption / task requirement / access obstacle. Read Kai’s case in three chunks. Accept a spoken enquiry plan and fade the classification prompts.
teacher.stretch: Explain how one assumption could create a structural barrier, then separate actions a learner can take from changes requiring provider or employer responsibility.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when the pupil challenges an assumption with evidence, accurately identifies an obstacle or requirement, and proposes a specific enquiry with no unsupported guarantee.

resources.title: Kai’s enquiry — full fictional case
resources.instructions: Analyse the case; no pupil must disclose identity, discrimination or financial circumstances.
items: Kai is interested in vehicle maintenance and has shown careful practical fault-finding during school projects.
The nearest provider described in the scenario has a start time that does not match the available bus service.
An adult comments, “That course is not for people from your background.”
Kai has not yet checked the provider’s current entry criteria, other routes or any transport support.
The card contains no evidence that Kai cannot learn the required skills. It also does not guarantee acceptance or a funded solution.
answers: Stereotype: group-background assumption.
Practical barrier: timing and transport.
Next step: provider/adviser enquiry, with actual options left unconfirmed.

resources.title: Diverse fictional examples
resources.instructions: Use one case to challenge an assumption while retaining genuine requirements.
items: Noor uses a wheelchair, follows a technical checking sequence and works at an accessible practice bench. The exact role and arrangements need investigation.
Elliot is male, interested in care work and practises calm, respectful communication. Training and actual role duties still matter.
Jules speaks little in large groups but contributes written plans and responds carefully in a project team.
No case is a real biography or a promise about recruitment.
answers: Noor challenges an automatic disability exclusion.
Elliot challenges a gender restriction on care.
Jules shows that team contribution can have several forms.
Use task evidence rather than identity or appearance to judge an exploration option.

lessons.title: Transferable skills and employability evidence
lessons.big_question: Which actions show skills that transfer across tasks?
lessons.objective: I can select evidence for communication, teamwork, problem-solving, organisation and digital skills.
success: I can select evidence for five named skills.
I can write three specific evidence statements.
I can identify one development need and a feasible practice action.

vocabulary.meaning: An ability useful across different tasks and settings.
Examples of relevant abilities and actions; not proof of being ready for every job.
Detailed enough to show what actually happened.
An area to practise or gather more evidence about.

slides.title: Transferable skills: evidence
body: Which actions show skills that transfer across tasks?
I can select evidence for communication, teamwork, problem-solving, organisation and digital skills.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct GROW Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: Does “I did DT” identify a transferable skill?
What could we say about the action instead?
slides.prompt: Give one specific improvement.
slides.answer: Describe the person’s contribution: measured parts, checked a list, explained a plan or shared agreed tasks.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Choose evidence, not impressive labels
body: Communication, teamwork, problem-solving, organisation and digital skills can appear across subjects.
Name context and individual action; add a result only if known.
Missing evidence means a question or practice need, not proven inability.
slides.prompt: Can the same activity show more than one skill?
slides.answer: Yes. Match each skill to the detail that supports it rather than copying one vague claim into every row.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 7 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Sam’s exhibition project
body: Sam agreed roles, checked a checklist and explained the plan.
Sam asked staff about a safe alternative for missing material.
Sam formatted a title in a document and saved it in the project folder.
slides.prompt: Which action provides the digital evidence?
slides.answer: Formatting the title and saving the file. This version explicitly includes digital actions; do not infer them from a poster alone.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Write three evidence statements
body: Organisation: checked the materials list before starting.
Teamwork: agreed roles with a partner and completed the agreed part.
Digital: formatted a title and saved the file in the project folder.
slides.prompt: How could you make one statement more precise without inventing a result?
slides.answer: Add the named context and stated action. Do not add perfect accuracy, speed or independent working unless observed.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: Identify a sensible development action
body: A: “Become perfect at technology by tomorrow.”
B: “Practise naming and finding one project file next ICT lesson.”
slides.prompt: Which action is manageable and checkable?
slides.answer: B. It names a small task and review point; use a checklist or adult prompt if needed.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Build a five-skill evidence bank: Use personal safe examples or Sam’s full card; mark the choice.
2. Write three strong statements: Choose three rows and write context + what the person did + link to skill.
3. Plan one development step: Identify a skill with limited evidence or one you want to practise.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 13 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can select evidence for five named skills.
I can write three specific evidence statements.
I can identify one development need and a feasible practice action.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when all five skills have considered evidence, three statements name specific actions and one realistic development step has a review point. Honest unknowns are acceptable and guide follow-up.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Transferable-skills evidence bank.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Give one specific skill statement and one feasible development action.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: Sam formatted and saved a title file during the exhibition project, showing digital skill. Next step: practise finding and reopening the file next ICT lesson.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: Transferable skills and employability evidence — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Build a five-skill evidence bank
tasks.prompt: Use personal safe examples or Sam’s full card; mark the choice.
items: Communication / context and action.
Teamwork / context and action.
Problem-solving / context and action.
Organisation / context and action.
Digital / context and action.
tasks.answer: Sam: explained plan; agreed and completed shared roles; checked a safe alternative with staff; used checklist; formatted and saved title. Different skills need their own action details.

tasks.heading: 2. Write three strong statements
tasks.prompt: Choose three rows and write context + what the person did + link to skill.
items: Statement 1…
Statement 2…
Statement 3…
Add a result only when the evidence supplies it.
tasks.answer: Examples: During the exhibition project Sam checked the materials list, showing organisation. Sam agreed and completed a shared role, showing teamwork. Sam formatted and saved a title file, showing digital skill.

tasks.heading: 3. Plan one development step
tasks.prompt: Identify a skill with limited evidence or one you want to practise.
items: What needs practice or more evidence?
What small action could help?
How and when will you check progress?
tasks.answer: Sam has no evidence yet about finding the file again. Next ICT lesson, practise reopening a named file and ask a teacher to observe. Do not call missing evidence a proven inability.

worksheet.exit_question: Give one specific skill statement and one feasible development action.
worksheet.exit_answer: Sam formatted and saved a title file during the exhibition project, showing digital skill. Next step: practise finding and reopening the file next ICT lesson.

Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

I Do: explain and model using the supplied case

misconceptions: Being in a lesson proves every relevant skill → identify an action.
The group’s success proves every member’s role → state the individual contribution.
No evidence means no ability → plan an observation or practice opportunity.
teacher.support: Offer five rows with verbs to choose from. Rehearse one statement, then fade the sentence frame for the next two. Record case analysis separately from personal skills evidence.
teacher.stretch: Evaluate which of two examples best supports a skill, explain the limits of both and identify the observation that would resolve uncertainty.

Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
