resources.title: Sam’s exhibition-project evidence
resources.instructions: Complete fictional case. This differs from the BUILD display case by explicitly supplying digital actions.
items: Sam checked a materials checklist before the group began.
Sam agreed who would measure and who would arrange the display, then completed the agreed part.
Sam explained the plan to the group and listened to one suggested change.
A material was missing; Sam asked staff to check whether an alternative was safe and suitable.
Sam used a document editor to format a title, then saved the file in the project folder.
The record does not say whether Sam could later find the file again, how quickly the work was done or how much prompting was used.
answers: Organisation, teamwork, communication, problem-solving and digital skills all have stated actions.
Do not invent independence, speed, perfect accuracy or a successful file-reopening result.
A future check can provide missing evidence.

resources.title: Evidence and practice planner
resources.instructions: Use one row per skill. A short accurate statement is enough.
items: Communication: sharing information, listening or using an agreed communication aid.
Teamwork: own contribution to a joint task.
Problem-solving: a stated problem and a suitable response.
Organisation: a plan, sequence, checklist or managed resource.
Digital: purposeful use of a device or software.
Practice plan: one skill → one small action → support/source → a check or review time.
answers: A subject can provide a context but is not itself evidence of a skill.
A digital or communication skill can be demonstrated with support; record the support accurately.
A practice action should create useful evidence, not promise mastery immediately.

lessons.title: Exploring career families
lessons.big_question: How can we compare career areas without treating a score as a prediction?
lessons.objective: I can compare at least three career areas and explain which two I want to investigate further.
success: I can compare at least three career areas.
I can justify two to investigate using at least two criteria.
I can keep unknown information separate from a poor fit.

vocabulary.meaning: A broad group of related roles, with differences within it.
A feature used to compare options.
A small set of options for further investigation.
Information not yet available; it is not a negative score.

slides.title: Exploring career families
body: How can we compare career areas without treating a score as a prediction?
I can compare at least three career areas and explain which two I want to investigate further.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct GROW Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: Does enjoying games prove someone wants to design them?
Does one job describe every role in a career family?
slides.prompt: Explain one limit.
slides.answer: No. Playing and creating involve different tasks. Broad families contain varied roles and conditions.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Compare, question, shortlist
body: Use interests, skill evidence, values and working conditions as separate criteria.
Record supported / possible / mismatch / unknown, with a reason.
A comparison helps select questions; it does not predict a perfect job.
slides.prompt: Why should “unknown” not mean zero ability or poor fit?
slides.answer: There is no evidence either way. A question is needed before judging fit.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 7 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Jordan’s profile
body: Jordan enjoys repairing models, explaining steps and solving a digital puzzle.
Jordan uses checklists, values helpful teams and likes visible results.
Jordan’s preferences about outdoor work and shifts are unknown.
slides.prompt: Which three families could be worth comparing?
slides.answer: Construction/engineering, people/care and creative/digital are plausible. Business/organisation could also be justified through checklists. No family is compulsory.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Compare three areas
body: Engineering: practical making is supported; exact role conditions remain unknown.
People/care: explanation and helpful teams offer clues; professional duties need investigation.
Creative/digital: puzzle interest gives a question; digital creation interest is not yet stated.
slides.prompt: Which judgement needs the most extra evidence?
slides.answer: Creative/digital needs checking whether Jordan enjoys creating with digital tools, not only playing. Other families also need actual role research.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: Keep uncertainty visible
body: A: “No shift information means poor fit.”
B: “Mark shifts unknown and ask what a particular role involves.”
slides.prompt: Which is a better comparison method?
slides.answer: B. A missing fact is not a mismatch. Avoid adding scores to produce a compulsory career.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Compare three career families: Use Jordan or your own profile and choose three from the six cards.
2. Shortlist two areas: Explain each choice using at least two criteria.
3. Test the shortlist: Write a question that could confirm or change each shortlisted option.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 13 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can compare at least three career areas.
I can justify two to investigate using at least two criteria.
I can keep unknown information separate from a poor fit.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when three families are compared, two shortlisted with two criteria each, and unknowns remain explicit. Reasoning is assessed; numerical ranking or a particular occupation is not required.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Career-family comparison grid.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Justify two areas with two criteria each, then name one unknown.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: For Jordan: engineering links practical making and problem-solving; people/care links explaining and a helpful-team value. Specific tasks, routes and conditions still need checking.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: Exploring career families — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Compare three career families
tasks.prompt: Use Jordan or your own profile and choose three from the six cards.
items: For each: interest fit / skill evidence / values fit / working conditions.
Use supported / possible / mismatch / unknown and give a short reason for every judgement.
tasks.answer: For Jordan, engineering has practical-interest evidence; people/care has explanation/helpful-team evidence; creative/digital has a possible puzzle/problem-solving link but creation interest is unknown. Specific role conditions remain unknown.

tasks.heading: 2. Shortlist two areas
tasks.prompt: Explain each choice using at least two criteria.
items: Area 1… because criterion… and criterion…
Area 2… because criterion… and criterion…
One area not prioritised yet… because…
tasks.answer: Engineering: making interest plus checklist/problem-solving evidence. People/care: explaining interest plus helpful-team values. Other pairs accepted with evidence; not prioritised yet does not mean permanently ruled out.

tasks.heading: 3. Test the shortlist
tasks.prompt: Write a question that could confirm or change each shortlisted option.
items: Question for area 1…
Question for area 2…
Which answer might change your view?
tasks.answer: Engineering: What tasks and conditions are involved in a specific technician role? People/care: How much time involves direct support, records or teamwork? Answers may alter fit; do not invent them.

worksheet.exit_question: Justify two areas with two criteria each, then name one unknown.
worksheet.exit_answer: For Jordan: engineering links practical making and problem-solving; people/care links explaining and a helpful-team value. Specific tasks, routes and conditions still need checking.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: Construction/engineering, people/care and creative/digital are plausible. Business/organisation could also be justified through checklists. No family is compulsory. Creative/digital needs checking whether Jordan enjoys creating with digital tools, not only playing. Other families also need actual role research.
misconceptions: A family is one job → identify several roles within it.
Unknown means unsuitable → preserve a question.
A quiz result is a command → suggestions need comparison and real evidence.
teacher.support: Provide Jordan’s card and three preselected families. Start with two criteria, then complete the other two with sentence stems and oral reasoning. Record unknown rather than guessing.
teacher.stretch: Compare two roles within one family and explain why their actual tasks could lead to different fit judgements. Use optional National Careers Service profiles with teacher support.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when three families are compared, two shortlisted with two criteria each, and unknowns remain explicit. Reasoning is assessed; numerical ranking or a particular occupation is not required.

resources.title: Six career-family exploration cards
resources.instructions: Original broad prompts, not exhaustive sector definitions or current role specifications. A role may connect with more than one family. Check a specific role before making decisions.
items: People & Care: examples include education, health support and social care. Explore communication, supporting others, records and teamwork; tasks and training vary.
Creative & Digital: examples include design, media and software. Explore making content, testing ideas and digital problem-solving; playing a game alone does not show interest in creating one.
Construction & Engineering: examples include trades, technical maintenance and manufacturing. Explore practical or technical tasks, checks and problem-solving; roles differ greatly.
Business & Organisation: examples include administration, retail coordination and logistics. Explore planning, records, customer communication or movement of materials.
Environment & Outdoors: examples include horticulture, conservation and animal-related work. Explore practical tasks, observations and records; some roles mix indoor and outdoor work.
Public & Community: examples include local services and public administration. Explore service, procedures, communication and organisation; requirements vary by role.
answers: No family has one fixed personality, gender, working pattern or entry route.
Use the cards to choose a specific role and questions for later investigation, not to claim current vacancies or guaranteed access.

resources.title: Jordan and the comparison key
resources.instructions: Fictional profile. Use all four criteria and keep missing information visible.
items: Jordan repairs small models in school projects and enjoys seeing a working result.
Jordan explains practical steps to a classmate and likes being helpful.
Jordan checks materials against a list and persists with digital puzzles.
Jordan values helpful, respectful teams and clear instructions.
Outdoor-work preferences, shift preferences and interest in making digital content are not stated.
Key: supported = direct evidence; possible = plausible link to test; mismatch = an evidenced conflict to investigate; unknown = no information yet.
answers: Engineering and people/care have several plausible links; creative/digital needs distinguishing puzzle play from content creation.
A mismatch is provisional and should prompt questions about role variation or support.
Do not total these labels into an aptitude score.

lessons.title: My career profile and enquiry plan
lessons.big_question: What evidence and questions should guide my next investigation?
lessons.objective: I can produce a profile, shortlist 2–3 career areas and set questions that will help me test whether they suit me.
success: I can synthesise strengths and skills with specific evidence.
I can justify a shortlist of two or three areas.
I can plan enquiries that could confirm or change my thinking.

vocabulary.meaning: Bring evidence together to make a coherent account.
A current summary that can change with new information.
Questions, sources and actions for investigating an option.
An agreed time to reconsider evidence and next steps.

slides.title: My career profile and enquiry plan
body: What evidence and questions should guide my next investigation?
I can produce a profile, shortlist 2–3 career areas and set questions that will help me test whether they suit me.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct GROW Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: Find one specific action, one value and one unknown in earlier work.
No earlier sheets? Use Sam’s complete evidence card.
slides.prompt: Which claim needs checking before it enters the profile?
slides.answer: A claim without a stated action, or an inferred preference, needs evidence or an unknown label.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Build a profile with limits
body: Summarise strengths, skills, interests and helpful conditions.
Choose two or three areas using at least two criteria each.
Include uncertainty; a useful plan can change your mind.
slides.prompt: Should the final profile hide a possible mismatch?
slides.answer: No. A mismatch or unknown helps identify the next question. It is not a reason for shame or an automatic rejection.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 7 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Sam’s profile — evidence first
body: Sam plans materials, explains steps, revises a model and formats a title file.
Sam enjoys practical making, food tasks and visible results.
Clear written steps and opportunities to ask questions help.
slides.prompt: Suggest a supported profile summary and its limits.
slides.answer: Sam shows organisation, communication, practical problem-solving and digital actions in projects. Practical food or design/maintenance roles may merit investigation; actual tasks, routes and conditions are unknown.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Make enquiries decision-useful
body: Role: What does a typical day involve?
Route: Which current entry routes apply to this specific role?
Conditions: What support or working arrangements should be discussed?
slides.prompt: How can the answer change a shortlist?
slides.answer: If tasks differ from Sam’s expectations, another role may fit better. Provider-specific route or support information must be checked rather than assumed.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: An action plan or a wish?
body: A: “Get my perfect job.”
B: “Next lesson, compare two role profiles with staff and record one fact and question for each.”
slides.prompt: Which is actionable and reviewable?
slides.answer: B states a manageable action, support and time. It gathers evidence without guaranteeing an outcome.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Synthesise the profile: Use your portfolio or Sam’s complete case. Label the choice.
2. Justify a shortlist: Select two or three areas with two criteria for each; record a possible mismatch or unknown.
3. Write an enquiry plan: Include three purposeful questions, a source or person and one timed next action.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 13 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can synthesise strengths and skills with specific evidence.
I can justify a shortlist of two or three areas.
I can plan enquiries that could confirm or change my thinking.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Summative review: four strengths, two evidence examples, skills/interests/values/conditions, two or three justified areas, one explicit unknown and three decision-useful enquiries with source and next action. Record secure/developing/next step, not a career-aptitude score.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Completed career profile and enquiry plan.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Give one justified area, one question that could change your view and a specific next action.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: Sam could investigate practical design because making and revision are evidenced. Ask about typical tasks; next lesson compare two role profiles and record what changes the shortlist.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: My career profile and enquiry plan — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Synthesise the profile
tasks.prompt: Use your portfolio or Sam’s complete case. Label the choice.
items: Four strengths and two specific evidence examples.
Transferable skills, interests and values.
Working conditions or support that help.
Write a two- or three-sentence profile summary.
tasks.answer: Sam: organisation, communication, persistence/problem-solving, practical/digital skill. Evidence: checked materials and revised a model; formatted and saved a file. Summary must not invent qualifications or permanent traits.

tasks.heading: 2. Justify a shortlist
tasks.prompt: Select two or three areas with two criteria for each; record a possible mismatch or unknown.
items: Area / strength or skill evidence / interest or value / condition or unknown.
Which area would you investigate first, and why?
tasks.answer: Catering and practical design/maintenance link making/food interests and organisation/problem-solving. Digital design could be investigated if creating digital work is of interest. Actual roles, entry routes and conditions remain unknown.

tasks.heading: 3. Write an enquiry plan
tasks.prompt: Include three purposeful questions, a source or person and one timed next action.
items: Ask about actual role tasks.
Ask about current routes or training.
Ask about workplace conditions, progression or possible support.
For each: how could an answer confirm or change the shortlist?
tasks.answer: Use teacher-supported National Careers Service role profiles for tasks, actual provider information for routes, and a school careers adviser/provider contact for questions. Next lesson compare two roles and review one fact and one unknown per role.

worksheet.exit_question: Give one justified area, one question that could change your view and a specific next action.
worksheet.exit_answer: Sam could investigate practical design because making and revision are evidenced. Ask about typical tasks; next lesson compare two role profiles and record what changes the shortlist.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: Sam shows organisation, communication, practical problem-solving and digital actions in projects. Practical food or design/maintenance roles may merit investigation; actual tasks, routes and conditions are unknown. If tasks differ from Sam’s expectations, another role may fit better. Provider-specific route or support information must be checked rather than assumed.
misconceptions: A profile must sound certain → well-stated uncertainty improves enquiry.
A source always answers every question → identify provider-specific or unanswered details.
Completing a classroom pack fulfils every careers duty → it is teaching evidence, not whole-school compliance.
teacher.support: Provide the complete Sam case and profile headings. Build a two-area shortlist before adding an optional third. Use a three-row question grid and one model; fade prompts for subsequent rows.
teacher.stretch: Identify an answer that would lead you to revise or drop a shortlisted area, and explain how you would verify that answer using an appropriate current source.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Summative review: four strengths, two evidence examples, skills/interests/values/conditions, two or three justified areas, one explicit unknown and three decision-useful enquiries with source and next action. Record secure/developing/next step, not a career-aptitude score.

resources.title: Sam’s complete evidence portfolio
resources.instructions: Fictional alternative for absent pupils or those choosing privacy. This supports analysis, not a personal vocational assessment.
items: Sam checked materials against a list before a classroom food project.
Sam explained practical steps to a partner and listened to feedback.
Sam built a card model, then revised it after feedback so its parts fitted.
Sam formatted a display title in a document editor and saved the file in the project folder.
Sam enjoys practical making, food projects and a visible finished result; helpful teamwork and clear expectations matter.
Written steps and time for questions support Sam’s participation.
Sam has not researched specific role tasks, current entry routes, schedules, progression or available adjustments.
answers: Possible strengths/skills: organisation, communication, problem-solving/persistence, practical and digital actions.
Two specific evidence examples can support several carefully stated skills.
Areas are provisional; unknowns should generate enquiries.

resources.title: Enquiry-plan and review checklist
resources.instructions: Use three rows: question / source or person / how the answer could affect the shortlist. Add a next action and review point.
items: Role question: What are the actual tasks in a named role? Source: a current National Careers Service role profile; note title and date checked.
Route question: What current routes or entry criteria apply? Source: the actual provider or course information, checked with school careers staff where needed.
Conditions question: What working arrangements or support could be discussed? Source: appropriate provider or careers adviser; availability is not assumed.
Next action: compare two role profiles next Careers lesson with staff support.
Review: one supported fact and one unresolved question per role; adjust shortlist if evidence changes.
Assessment: profile evidence, justified shortlist, explicit uncertainty and feasible enquiries.
answers: A research plan is not an application or permission to contact an external person. Follow the school’s normal arrangements for contact.
The optional websites support later enquiry; the paper case fully supports today’s task.
Classroom completion is not an accredited award, employer encounter or personal guidance meeting.
